opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is that it lowers the barrier to asking questions. When I was a student, if you got stuck on something in a textbook, you either had to find a professor during office hours, ask a friend who might be just as confused, or just sit there staring at the page. A lot of young people, especially the shy ones or the ones without access to good mentors, would simply give up at that point. Now you can ask as many "dumb" questions as you want, at two in the morning, and get a patient, reasonable explanation. That's really powerful.

As a mathematician, I also see it changing how students engage with proofs and problem solving. You can ask the model to explain a step you don't understand, or to show you a different approach, or to give you a simpler example first. That kind of interactive, personalized scaffolding used to be available only to students with very good tutors.

That said, I do think there's a real risk if it's used the wrong way. Learning science, and especially mathematics, requires struggle. You have to wrestle with a problem yourself to really internalize it. If a student just asks for the answer and copies it down, they're not learning much. So I think the skill young people need to develop is using these tools as a thinking partner rather than an answer machine: try it yourself first, then use the model to check your reasoning, find your mistakes, or push you further.

And looking ahead, I'm genuinely excited. Students who learn to work alongside AI will be able to explore much more ambitious questions much earlier in their careers. The frontier of what a motivated young person can reach on their own is moving forward quite a bit, and I think we'll see some remarkable work come out of that generation.

r001.rationale: The response describes anytime access to patient explanations and personalized help, and says AI lets students reach more ambitious questions earlier.

r002.rationale: The response says students must wrestle with problems themselves to internalize learning and cautions against simply copying answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's changing learning in two directions at once, and which one you get depends a lot on how the student uses it.

The optimistic side is something I've seen firsthand with my own students. The biggest barrier to learning science has never really been access to information. Textbooks have existed for a long time. The barrier is that when you get stuck, you need someone to talk to, and most students don't have a patient expert sitting next to them at eleven at night. Now they do, in some form. A student can ask "why does this step follow from that one" and get an answer tailored to exactly where their confusion is. That kind of individualized back-and-forth used to be a privilege reserved for people with great mentors or small seminar classes. Making it widely available is a genuinely big deal.

The other side is that science is learned by struggling. The understanding comes from sitting with a problem you can't solve, trying wrong approaches, and slowly building intuition. If a student uses the model to skip that struggle, to just get the answer and move on, they'll feel like they're learning and they won't be. That's the failure mode I worry about, and I think it's a real one, especially for younger students who haven't yet developed a sense of what real understanding feels like.

So the way I frame it for students is: use it as a tutor, not as an oracle. Ask it to explain, to check your reasoning, to give you a hint rather than the solution. Argue with it. One thing I actually encourage is to try to catch it being wrong, because it does make mistakes in mathematics and physics, and the act of verifying what it says is itself excellent training. That skepticism is a core scientific skill, and it's one that this technology, used well, can help develop rather than erode.

Longer term, I think it shifts what we should emphasize in science education. Rote computation and memorization are going to matter less. Asking good questions, knowing what a correct answer should look like, and being able to judge whether an argument holds together are going to matter more. Those were always the important skills. The tools are just making that more obvious.

r001.rationale: The response says students can get tailored explanations and back-and-forth help when stuck, making individualized science support widely available.

r002.rationale: The response says science learning requires struggling with problems and warns that students cannot skip that work by simply taking the answer.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is that students can ask questions without feeling embarrassed. When you’re learning science, you often get stuck on something that seems basic, and in a classroom you may hesitate to raise your hand. With ChatGPT, you can say, “I don’t understand. Can you explain that another way?” And you can keep going until you find an explanation that makes sense to you.

But there’s a difference between understanding an explanation and being able to reason through a problem yourself. If students use it just to get answers, they can miss the learning. A more useful interaction is, “Give me a hint,” or, “Here’s my reasoning—where does it go wrong?”

And science is about checking ideas against evidence. ChatGPT can make mistakes, so I’d want young people to treat its answers as things to investigate. Use it to develop a question, make a prediction, and then test that prediction. That’s where it could help students become more curious and independent.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated, on-demand explanations, but does not communicate that this accelerates science learning.

r002.rationale: It says students need to reason through problems and test predictions, but does not clearly state that learning still requires hard work from the learner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is that young people can ask questions without feeling embarrassed. If you don’t understand an explanation, you can ask again, ask for an example, or say, “Can you explain that in a different way?” That can make science feel much more accessible.

But learning science also means learning how to check an answer. So I’d encourage students to use ChatGPT to make predictions, work through their reasoning, and then compare those ideas with experiments or evidence. The exciting possibility is that it helps students become more curious and more willing to investigate questions for themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes asking for repeated or alternative explanations as making science more accessible, but does not communicate that this access can accelerate learning.

r002.rationale: The response encourages students to check answers, reason through ideas, and investigate, but does not clearly state that learning science still requires hard work from the learner.
